evidenceAudit.scope: Adolescents and adults with chronic asthma in primary and specialist care: diagnosis, control assessment with the Asthma Control Test (ACT), SINA stepwise treatment, inhaler regimens and referral for severe asthma. Verified against the Saudi Initiative for Asthma (SINA) 2024 update; inhaler doses and contraindications from US FDA prescribing information. Acute attacks are covered in the Acute Asthma topic.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: SINA medication appendix (exact low/medium/high ICS dose bands) not extracted — tables not available as text

pathophysiology.summary: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable respiratory symptoms (wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough) and variable expiratory airflow limitation. Most adults have type 2 (eosinophilic/allergic) inflammation, which is steroid-responsive.
keyMechanisms: Allergen or irritant exposure → type 2 inflammation (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; eosinophils, IgE, mast cells) → bronchial hyper-responsiveness, mucus and oedema.
Airway smooth muscle constriction is reversible with bronchodilators; persistent inflammation causes remodelling and fixed obstruction if under-treated.
ICS treats the underlying inflammation — the cornerstone at every step (SINA); SABA alone increases exacerbation and death risk.
Type 2 biomarkers (blood eosinophils 150/µL or more, FeNO 20 ppb or more) predict ICS and biologic response (SINA).

symptoms: Episodic wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough — worse at night or early morning.
Triggers: allergens (dust mite, pets, pollen), exercise, cold air, viral infections, smoke, dust storms.
Associated rhinitis, eczema, family history of atopy.
redFlags: Severe exacerbation in the past 12 months or prior ICU admission/intubation
Using more than 3 SABA canisters a year
Needing more than 12 inhalations/day of ICS-formoterol reliever for 2–3 days
precipitants: Allergen exposure, dust storms, smoke, vaping
Aspirin/NSAIDs (in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease); non-selective beta-blockers

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Older smoker; persistent post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7; less reversibility.
Inspiratory stridor; normal spirometry between episodes.
Chronic sputum, CT changes, very high IgE/eosinophils.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: FEV1/FVC reduced; FEV1 rises 12% or more and 200 mL or more after bronchodilator.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms asthma; a normal test when well does not exclude it — repeat when symptomatic or use PEF variability.
ruleIn.normalValue: FEV1/FVC above lower limit of normal; post-bronchodilator FEV1 change below 12%

clinicalManagement.title: Start treatment by ACT score (adults and adolescents)
actions: ACT 20 or more (step 1): as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol; alternative as-needed SABA with low-dose ICS from separate inhalers. SABA alone is no longer recommended.
Daily low-dose ICS (with or without LABA) if symptoms more than twice a week, exacerbation risk factors or fixed obstruction.
ACT 16–19 (step 2): daily low-dose ICS/LABA with a reliever.
ACT below 16 (step 3): daily medium-dose ICS/LABA with a reliever; if early exacerbation signs add prednisolone 30–60 mg for 3–5 days.

clinicalManagement.title: Stepwise adjustment
actions: Step 2: low-dose ICS/LABA (alternative: low-dose ICS plus LTRA, especially with rhinitis).
Step 3: medium-dose ICS/LABA (alternative: add tiotropium to ICS if LABA cannot be used). Refer to an asthma specialist if hard to control.
Step 4: add a LAMA — single-inhaler triple therapy (e.g. fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol 200/62.5/25 µg once daily).
Step 5: specialist; biologics by phenotype — omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, dupilumab; lowest possible OCS if biologics unsuitable.
Before stepping up check adherence, inhaler technique, triggers and comorbidities (rhinosinusitis, GERD, obesity).

clinicalManagement.title: ICS-formoterol MART
actions: Budesonide-formoterol: 1 inhalation twice daily (step 2) or 2 inhalations twice daily (step 3), plus extra inhalations as reliever up to 12 inhalations/day (SINA).
Maximum formoterol 72 µg/day; needing this for 2–3 days means seek review.
With a non-formoterol LABA (salmeterol, vilanterol, indacaterol) use SABA as reliever. Never LABA or LAMA without ICS.

clinicalManagement.title: Step down
actions: Reduce ICS gradually every 3–6 months to the lowest dose that maintains control; do not stop LABA abruptly in a patient on ICS/LABA.
Seasonal asthma: start low-dose ICS before the season.

clinicalManagement.title: Reduce risk
actions: Written action plan; check reliever use (more than 3 SABA canisters a year = high risk).
Stop smoking and vaping; annual influenza vaccination; treat rhinitis.
Long-term OCS: calcium, vitamin D and bone protection if osteoporosis risk; increase steroid at times of stress.

learningObjectives: Diagnose asthma, assess control with the ACT and manage it stepwise using SINA 2024.

keyPoints: ICS at every step; no SABA-only treatment.
ACT score chooses the starting step.
MART: one inhaler for maintenance and relief, max 12 inhalations/day.
Check adherence and technique before stepping up.
Refer severe asthma for phenotyping and biologics.
pitfalls: Stepping up without checking inhaler technique.
Stopping LABA abruptly in a patient on ICS/LABA.

patientEducation: Inhaler technique at every visit; spacer with MDI.
Trigger avoidance, including dust storms and smoke.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular exercise; weight loss if obese.
mdtReferrals: Asthma specialist if uncontrolled at step 3 or above, or diagnostic doubt.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review 1–3 months after starting or changing treatment, then every 3–12 months when controlled; spirometry periodically; specialist referral if uncontrolled at step 3 or above.
